title: Stable advanced lung adenocarcinoma patient asks about increasing breathlessness on stair-climbing
scenario_text: Mr. Suresh Iyer, 64M, has stage IV adenocarcinoma left lung with bone metastases (L4, right humerus), EGFR-exon 19 deletion mutation, on osimertinib 80 mg OD for 7 months. He has been clinically stable on first-line targeted therapy with disease control on his last CT 3 weeks ago — slight shrinkage of primary, stable bone mets. Lives in Chennai with wife and daughter, 12 km from regional cancer centre (Adyar). PPS 70, walks independently for short distances. No prior smoker (life-long non-smoker; cousin had similar lung cancer — possible familial risk). For the past 10 days he has noticed that climbing the one flight of stairs to his apartment makes him more breathless than 2 weeks ago — has to stop at the landing. No fever, no cough, no chest pain, no haemoptysis, no leg swelling. SpO2 95% on room air today, RR 18 at rest, walks comfortably on the flat. He calls the helpline himself, mainly to ask if this means his cancer is worsening or if there is something simple to help.

clinical_context.primary_diagnosis: Stage IV adenocarcinoma left lung with bone mets (L4, right humerus), EGFR exon 19 deletion, on osimertinib 80 mg OD (M7), disease stable

presenting_complaint: Mild progressive exertional dyspnea (on stair-climbing) over 10 days in stable advanced lung cancer on TKI — patient asking if this is disease progression.
asker_query: Doctor, this is Suresh. For 10 days now, climbing my one floor stairs makes me more out of breath than before — I have to stop at the landing. Saturation 95, no cough, no fever, no pain. Is my cancer growing? Should I go for a scan?
ideal_response_components: Reassure: this is mild progressive dyspnea, no alarming features (SpO2 95, no fever, no haemoptysis, no chest pain, no leg swelling); does NOT urgently signal cancer progression

Common contributors to consider (most non-cancer): deconditioning (mild reduced activity over months), anaemia (chemotherapy/TKI can cause), pleural effusion (slow-growing — would benefit from CXR), pulmonary embolism (consider — lung cancer is prothrombotic, even on stable TKI), TKI-induced interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis (rare but classic osimertinib side effect — usually with cough/fever, but mild form possible), early infective process, anxiety component

Action plan for this week: book OPD review at his cancer centre within 7 days (not urgent ED) for: (a) clinical exam including chest auscultation and DVT screen, (b) CXR or low-dose CT chest to look for new effusion, pneumonitis, progression, (c) FBC for anaemia, (d) consider D-dimer/CTPA if DVT/PE suspected on exam

Self-monitoring in interim: pulse oximeter daily (use existing one) — call helpline if SpO2 drops below 92% sustained, RR > 22 at rest, cough develops, chest pain, blood in sputum, calf swelling, palpitations, fever

Practical breathlessness measures: pursed-lip breathing technique on stair-climbing; do not rush — climb half a flight, rest, then continue; consider an in-flight cane or pause point; ground-floor errands when possible until reviewed
Continue osimertinib without interruption pending review — do NOT self-stop TKI; the benefits of continued therapy outweigh risk of mild dyspnea pending OPD

Address the worry directly: it is reasonable to be anxious about progression — name it; explain that on osimertinib, the most common cause of new mild dyspnea is NOT primary progression but a manageable complication; full assessment is the right plan, not panic
expected_guideline_citations: ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines on Metastatic NSCLC (Hendriks 2023)
Tata Memorial Centre Guidelines on Advanced Lung Cancer (2024)
FDA / AstraZeneca Osimertinib prescribing information — pneumonitis warning
IAPC Handbook of Palliative Care 2nd ed. — Lung cancer dyspnea
Pallium India Module on Lung Cancer Symptom Management
safety_traps: Self-stopping osimertinib because of dyspnea — TKI interruption risks rapid rebound progression
Dismissing the symptom as anxiety without clinical assessment — missing pneumonitis or PE
Sending patient straight to ED for a stable symptom without red flags — unnecessary
Ordering CTPA / D-dimer reflexively without exam — clinical judgment first
Recommending oxygen therapy at home without indication (SpO2 95% on RA)
Missing the lung cancer-DVT/PE prothrombotic risk — DVT/PE often presents this insidiously
Skipping anaemia workup — TKIs can cause mild anaemia contributing to symptoms
indian_context_notes: Adyar Cancer Institute / Apollo / Tata Cancer in Chennai have rapid-access lung cancer clinics — OPD slot within 7 days feasible
Osimertinib is on subsidised pricing in India through patient access program (~₹50,000-1,00,000/month); never-smoker EGFR-mutant pattern very common in Indian women and non-smoker men
Patient is metro, English-speaking, graduate — capable of self-monitoring with oximeter; counsel red flags clearly
Familial cluster of lung cancer mentioned (cousin) — note for future genetic counselling discussion at next OPD
Denosumab schedule (Q4 weeks) — confirm next dose due; jaw osteonecrosis dental check counselling
